segments.title: Constellation's off-the-shelf value problem
segments.summary: Constellation began as a conservative off-the-shelf frigate and drifted toward destroyer-level cost comparisons.
segments.body: The central procurement puzzle is how an off-the-shelf frigate with minimal-modification ambitions came to offer roughly 60 percent of a Burke's capability at 80 percent of its cost. At that price, decision-makers could reasonably ask why they should not buy another destroyer. Likely causes include the drive for technically perfect ships, political fear of losing ships, and acquisition criteria that reward additional safeguards and capabilities. The US Navy had also allowed a long gap to open after its last true frigates left service. Institutions and lost design practice shaped the FFG-62 problem alongside the choice of hull.

evidence.note: The transcript asks how a prudent off-the-shelf design became a poor value proposition against Burke cost and capability.
The discussion points to NAVSEA perfectionism, political loss aversion, procurement criteria, and the post-Perry frigate gap.

segments.title: Perry class as the basic frigate benchmark
segments.summary: The Oliver Hazard Perry class becomes the baseline for what a numerous, utilitarian US Navy frigate could be.
segments.body: Basic did not mean cheap or useless: the Perry class offered a sound hull, a functional weapons fit, and few unnecessary extras. Its consistently important capability was anti-submarine warfare, while the fleet accepted limits in other roles. Those limits were manageable because 51 ships supplied numbers for carrier-group screens, surface-action-group escorts, and convoy protection. A frigate could provide most of the required capability most of the time instead of trying to match a high-end combatant in every circumstance. That combination of specialization, availability, and acceptable performance is the benchmark used throughout the Constellation postmortem.

evidence.note: The transcript describes the Perry class as good, basic, utilitarian ships whose main constant capability was ASW.
The discussion emphasizes multiple hulls, 51 Perrys, and their carrier-battle-group, surface-action-group, and convoy escort roles.

segments.title: Post-Cold War transformation displaced the basic frigate
segments.summary: Post-Cold War technological ambitions help explain why the Navy moved away from a simple Perry successor and toward the Littoral Combat Ship.
segments.body: The Perrys did not fit a post-Cold War preference for highly visible technological transformation. Donald Rumsfeld's effort to make US forces so technologically advanced that they would deter challengers helped shape that preference. The Littoral Combat Ship emerged from a genuine desire for a flexible, fast vessel suited to inshore operations. Designs such as Denmark's Absalon and Iver Huitfeldt classes suggested that flexible mission arrangements could be useful. The strategic mistake was leaving no separate conventional frigate to handle escort work while the specialized littoral ship was developed.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the basic Perry with the post-Cold War pursuit of technological transformation associated with Donald Rumsfeld.
The discussion treats the LCS as an initially plausible flexible inshore concept and argues for separating it from a continued Perry-style frigate mission.

segments.title: LCS mission overload sets up the next frigate problem
segments.summary: Trying to make the Littoral Combat Ship perform both close-in rapid-response work and traditional frigate duties produced incompatible demands.
segments.body: A modernized Perry could have continued the unglamorous escort work while the LCS concentrated on fast, close-in support for littoral and amphibious operations. The LCS was also asked to perform traditional frigate duties. A design able to do both mission sets robustly was never likely to remain as small or inexpensive as promised. Repeated compromises affected both LCS variants without resolving the underlying concept. The diagnosis is overreach and over-specification rather than a lack of imagination, a pattern that the FFG(X) program would soon repeat in reverse.

evidence.note: The transcript says a Perry continuation could have handled frigate duties while the LCS focused on rapid littoral response and amphibious screening.
The discussion traces repeated LCS compromises and characterizes the result as overreach and over-specification before introducing FFG(X).

segments.title: FFG(X) requirements leave little room for later growth
segments.summary: The FFG(X) capability matrix is already crowded with present-day demands before the weapons and combat system are considered.
segments.body: The requirement chart is striking because so much of it is marked as an immediate capability rather than space for future growth. It is unclear why every offensive electronic-warfare function and boat-handling option had to be present from the first ship. A crewed MH-60R and an MQ-8 unmanned helicopter make sense for anti-submarine work, but they also require aviation facilities sized for both. Each demand is individually defensible, which is how the overall package becomes difficult to restrain. A frigate intended to be conservative was entering design with little room to defer attractive but nonessential features.

evidence.note: The transcript reviews the capability matrix and asks why several electronic-warfare functions could not remain growth options.
The discussion covers boat capacity and the planned combination of an MH-60R with an MQ-8 for the ASW role.

segments.title: VLS and Aegis expectations raise frigate cost
segments.summary: A few more missile cells are not the main cost driver, and the capability priorities look inverted for an ASW frigate.
segments.body: The proposed fit includes 32 Mark 41 VLS cells for SM-2 and ESSM Block 2, a 21-cell RAM launcher, a 57 mm gun, a fixed phased-array radar, and an Aegis-derived combat system. Most of the cost lies in the sensors, computers, power, and integration needed to make the launchers useful, whether the ship carries a handful of cells or several dozen. Fleet-common systems can pull a frigate toward destroyer-like cost even when each choice sounds prudent in isolation. The priority structure is more troubling: the fixed radar appears in the first tier while variable-depth and towed-array sonars appear in the second. A ship justified by anti-submarine warfare was being defined first by an expensive air-warfare ecosystem.

evidence.note: The transcript lists the 32-cell Mark 41 VLS, RAM, gun fit, and the computers and sensors behind missile-system cost.
The Navy's fleet-networking, phased-array radar, Aegis, aviation, weapons, and sonar requirements are reviewed, with ASW sonars placed in tier two.
The transcript contrasts cooperative engagement and traditional surface and ASW roles with an apparent emphasis on air-warfare systems.

segments.title: FFG(X) reverses the LCS mission graft
segments.summary: Where LCS had frigate duties added to a littoral ship, FFG(X) added littoral penetration and unmanned-system duties to a frigate.
segments.body: The Perry carried Standard missiles with a much simpler radar and fire-control arrangement than the proposed Aegis-family fit. FFG(X) was also expected to deploy unmanned systems into contested environments to gain sensor and weapons advantages. This repeats the LCS mistake from the opposite direction. LCS had conventional frigate work attached to its specialized littoral mission, while FFG(X) had the littoral mission attached to an already demanding frigate role. Combining the two sets of requirements forces each to pay for capabilities needed by the other and undermines the intended value of the hull.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the Perry's Standard-missile fit and Mark 92 system with the proposed Aegis-family approach.
The Navy's unmanned-system requirement leads to the argument that FFG(X) attached LCS duties to a frigate just as LCS had attached frigate duties to a littoral ship.

segments.title: The parent-design competition offered several kinds of risk reduction
segments.summary: The FFG(X) contestants ranged from an American cutter and LCS derivatives to established European frigates with very different strengths.
segments.body: The competition was intended to reduce risk by selecting a design that already existed in working form. On its face, Spain's Álvaro de Bazán class was an obvious match because it was already an Aegis frigate, though reputation and size could work against it. The MEKO A-200 offered a highly configurable menu, but that flexibility could invite a politically and administratively difficult fight over options and suppliers. The Freedom and Independence LCS derivatives carried the reputation of the program the Navy was trying to escape. The eventual FREMM choice came from a broad field of real ships rather than a lack of plausible alternatives.

evidence.note: The transcript introduces the competition, the Legend-class cutter proposal, and the Álvaro de Bazán F100 as an existing Aegis frigate.
The discussion compares the configurable MEKO approach with LCS derivatives whose program reputation made selection unlikely.

segments.title: FREMM was a sound parent design, not a ready-made US ASW frigate
segments.summary: FREMM is a flexible multi-mission frigate with strong ASW, while Type 26 is a purpose-built submarine hunter.
segments.body: Type 26 and FREMM reflect different design priorities. Type 26 is built around anti-submarine warfare and accepts limitations elsewhere, while FREMM is a general-purpose frigate that performs ASW well alongside other missions. For a US Navy planning to buy many ships, FREMM's greater flexibility could be a sensible advantage over a more specialized hunter. The competition also required functioning ships rather than paper proposals, which made the choice a genuine risk-reduction measure. Selecting a good multi-mission parent still left the Navy to decide which American mission and systems would dominate the derivative.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts Type 26 as a purpose-built ASW ship with FREMM as a multi-mission design possessing strong ASW capability.
The discussion explains why FREMM's flexibility and status as a ship already in service made selection reasonable for a large US program.

segments.title: European crewing assumptions complicated American adaptation
segments.summary: FREMM's European personnel model, automation, and systems architecture were not neutral features that could simply be retained under US Navy requirements.
segments.body: FREMM met NATO standards, but it was designed around European navies' smaller crews and recruitment constraints. Automation and ship-management systems help those crews sustain damage-control and operating functions with fewer people. The much larger US Navy recruits, retains, and structures careers differently, so it approaches crewing and survivability from another institutional baseline. Replacing European sensors with American radars then changes the superstructure and the placement of supporting equipment. A warship is a system of systems, so each major substitution changes relationships throughout the design and makes high commonality progressively less credible.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses European crewing, automation, damage control, retention, and the different personnel assumptions of the US Navy.
American radars and systems require structural changes, illustrating why a ship's connected systems make broad design substitution difficult.

segments.title: American systems and Burke-derived standards reshape the hull
segments.summary: Visible hull changes, added displacement, and high-end technical standards show how the FREMM derivative became a substantially different ship.
segments.body: American radar, sonar, and weapons choices changed the superstructure, hull lines, and internal relationships of the parent design. The derivative grew by about 500 tons and was lengthened by 23.6 feet, officially providing margin and room for future growth. NAVSEA's approach appears to have turned NATO standards up to their maximum level. Because the Navy had not built a true frigate for years, its most recent successful standards baseline was the Arleigh Burke destroyer rather than a restrained escort. That choice reduced the risk of repeating LCS weaknesses but also made Burke comparisons and high-end requirements difficult to escape.

evidence.note: The transcript identifies changed hull lines, roughly 500 tons of growth, a 23.6-foot length increase, and demanding naval standards.
The discussion links the frigate-construction gap to reliance on the Navy's latest successful destroyer standards and argues for a lower basic-frigate baseline.

segments.title: Task-group frigates and independent pickets need different designs
segments.summary: A light frigate that works inside a formation should not be specified as if it must stand alone on the fleet's outer screen.
segments.body: A light frigate that operates inside a task group is a different proposition from a larger frigate or destroyer expected to hold an outer picket station. The frigate can supply the anti-submarine specialization while the destroyer directs high-end air defence. The analogy is to Arethusa- and Atlanta-class light cruisers, useful formation ships that were not designed to duel larger cruisers or capital ships alone. Sending one against a Deutschland-class Panzerschiff would have misused it, even though both light cruiser classes fought effectively in the missions they were built for. Ship position and role should therefore be settled before sensors, weapons, and survivability standards are assigned.

evidence.note: The transcript distinguishes light-frigate task-group assets from picket-capable frigates and destroyers with different principal warfare roles.
Arethusa and Atlanta light cruisers illustrate useful formation ships that were not expected to fight larger cruisers or capital ships alone.

segments.title: Why construction continues on the first two Constellation hulls
segments.summary: Continued work on Constellation and Congress was intended to support the current yard while policymakers decide how to use its shipbuilding capacity.
segments.body: Cancellation did not immediately end work on the first two ships. Continued construction was reportedly intended to support the yard in the near term while policymakers decide how to use its shipbuilding capacity over the longer term. The choice separates the fate of the class from the industrial consequences of withdrawing work from a specialized builder. Congress must weigh fleet capability and funding against effects on the naval industrial base.

evidence.note: The quoted report says work on the first two FFG-62s continues in the near term to support the yard while policymakers decide how to use its shipbuilding capacity.
The transcript identifies fleet capability, funding, and the US shipbuilding industrial base as consequences of Congress's decision.

segments.title: The successor frigate needs a deliberately modest baseline
segments.summary: The post-cancellation plan points toward a Legend-class-derived first flight whose main purpose is to establish achievable frigate standards.
segments.body: The Congressional Research Service groups frigates, LCS, mine-warfare ships, and patrol craft together as small surface combatants despite their very different jobs. Its fleet plan describes 73 such combatants, including 58 future frigates and modified Flight II ships. The initial Legend-class-derived flight can be read as a muscular cutter that establishes a credible baseline before later flights add capability. The Oliver Hazard Perry appears in the report as a reminder that the Navy has previously built a useful, numerous frigate without making it a small destroyer. The successor should be capable, basic, and easy to procure in quantity rather than designed to impress in every mission area.

evidence.note: The transcript defines small surface combatants, cites the planned total and frigate component, and interprets Flight I as a baseline for Flight II.
The Perry image prompts an argument for a capable, basic, utilitarian frigate that performs its assigned job without unnecessary features.

segments.title: Four warfare missions turn the frigate into a high-end combatant
segments.summary: Constellation's formal mission list gives anti-air warfare and ASW near-equal weight rather than building the ship around one principal frigate role.
segments.body: The class was defined for anti-air, anti-surface, anti-submarine, and electromagnetic warfare in both blue-water and littoral settings, independently or in large formations. Anti-submarine warfare appears third in that list despite being a central reason for buying a frigate. Local self-defence differs from area air warfare, which requires a ship to protect other units across a wider space. A frigate normally has one principal warfare mission and supports secondary tasks with proportionate systems. Combining destroyer-level air warfare with demanding ASW brings the computers, power generation, space, and integration burden of two primary missions into one hull. For a fleet already rich in Burkes, making every escort Burke-like sacrifices the numbers needed to cover all the fleet's tasks.

evidence.note: The transcript lists the four warfare areas and identifies area anti-air warfare as the first destroyer-like requirement.
The discussion argues for ASW as the primary frigate role and explains the size, power, and cost burden of combining it with high-end air warfare.

segments.title: Point defence and area air warfare are not the same frigate mission
segments.summary: FFG-62's guided-missile designation carries a more demanding implication than the Perry's Cold War missile fit.
segments.body: Point-defence systems protect their own ship at short range, while area systems protect other ships and aircraft across a larger battlespace. US Navy designations add a G to ships equipped for area air defence, which gives FFG-62's label a specific meaning. The Perry also carried Standard missiles, but it used a single-arm launcher and lacked a complete Aegis package. Constellation paired VLS with an Aegis-derived system intended to participate in area air warfare. Projecting modern definitions backward can obscure how much the meaning and cost of a guided-missile frigate have changed.

evidence.note: The quoted footnote distinguishes short-range point defence from area air defence and explains the guided-missile designation.
The transcript contrasts the Perry's launcher and fire-control fit with FFG-62's Aegis and VLS package and warns against retroactive definitions.

segments.title: Burke standards made a mini-Burke comparison inevitable
segments.summary: Constellation was meant to support the fleet's air battle rather than replace a Burke, but its standards and systems made political comparison with the destroyer unavoidable.
segments.body: A widening knowledge gap separates naval professionals from the political decision-makers who approve procurement. The Spruance-to-Zumwalt comparison illustrates the gap: the Navy retained a Spruance-shaped requirement after that role had faded from the political picture of the fleet. Within Navy doctrine, FFG-62's missiles could support a cooperative engagement led by another Aegis ship without making the frigate an independent air-defence commander. The distinction is difficult to communicate when the ship carries Burke-derived standards, Aegis, Standard missiles, and a familiar guided-missile label. Constellation was not conceived as a mini-Burke, but the successful Burke program supplied the obvious technical and political benchmark. Deferring the more expansive air-warfare fit to a later flight could have protected the first ships from that comparison and established a clearer frigate identity.

evidence.note: The transcript discusses political-service knowledge gaps and air-warfare capability as a cooperative missile contribution linked to another Aegis ship.
The Spruance-to-Zumwalt comparison shows how a naval requirement can persist after its role has faded from the political picture of the fleet.
The class is not described as an intended mini-Burke, but Burke standards and familiar statistics invite that comparison.
The Navy's success in sustaining the Burke program makes it hard to differentiate other combatants, and the transcript suggests clearer tiers of air-warfare participation.

segments.title: An unstable procurement drumbeat erodes cost and yard confidence
segments.summary: Repeatedly changing annual orders left the program below its planned fleet total and made a second production yard increasingly unrealistic.
segments.body: The procurement table repeatedly promises higher future orders while buying roughly one ship per year through fiscal 2023. By fiscal 2024, the original trajectory would have placed nine ships on order, but the actual total was six before the fiscal 2025 cancellation. Plans for a second yard only made sense if annual procurement rose above two ships, a rate the program never sustained. Even the existing builder had reason to question whether continued investment in workforce and facilities would be rewarded. The lead ship's roughly $1.5 billion cost includes detailed design and other non-recurring engineering that later hulls should spread across a learning curve. Cutting and shifting the production rhythm prevents that curve and industrial capacity from delivering their intended savings.

evidence.note: The transcript follows changing annual plans, compares six actual orders with nine previously planned, and explains why a second yard never became viable.
The lead ship's cost includes design and non-recurring engineering, while unstable follow-on quantities prevent normal learning-curve reductions.

segments.title: Commonality collapsed as design changes accumulated
segments.summary: FREMM commonality fell from about 85 percent to roughly 15 percent as design changes accumulated.
segments.body: The parent-design rationale depended on preserving enough of FREMM to save design time and reduce technical risk. Official reporting put commonality at about 85 percent early in the program and roughly 15 percent after the alterations, a relationship too distant to provide the expected advantage. A 2021 description likened the derivative to a larger but essentially similar house, while the 2024 assessment showed that the Navy had effectively designed a new frigate. Overlay images show that even bridge position and layout changed despite earlier claims that this area would remain substantially intact. Requirements for American-built equipment and new sensors created individually understandable changes that cascaded through structure, internal spaces, and system relationships. The Navy also paid for design rights, then retained so little of the parent that a fact-finding study might have yielded the useful lessons without purchasing the design. By the time officials acknowledged that adapting another navy's design could be harder than starting fresh, Constellation no longer functioned as a modified repeat.

evidence.note: The transcript contrasts the original high-commonality premise with later reporting of roughly 15 percent and argues that the Navy had created a new ship.
Bridge and layout comparisons, American-built systems, and official admissions illustrate how cumulative changes erased the modified-repeat advantage.
The transcript argues that the Navy paid for design rights it barely used and could have learned the retained features through a fact-finding study.

segments.title: Construction began before the basic design stabilized
segments.summary: Two years into lead-ship construction, basic drawings were still changing and supposedly mature modules had to stop work for design reasons.
segments.body: A June 2025 assessment said the program still had not completed the functional design needed to demonstrate stability more than two years after construction began. The Navy and builder continued revising general-arrangement drawings and structural components on which later design work depended. The lead ship had moved to an April 2029 delivery, three years later than its original contract date. This sequence contradicts leading practice, which completes basic and functional design before cutting steel. The inconsistency becomes visible when modules reported as more than 90 percent designed are the same modules whose construction had to pause because the design changed. Progress percentages cannot compensate for an unsettled baseline.

evidence.note: The quoted assessment reports persistent design instability, a three-year delivery delay, and continuing revision of foundational drawings after construction began.
The discussion explains the importance of general-arrangement drawings and contrasts reported module maturity with pauses caused by design changes.

segments.title: Weight growth consumes capability reserved for the ship's future
segments.summary: A reported 759-metric-ton increase did more than enlarge the ship: it reduced the margin available for later weapons and sensors.
segments.body: By October 2024, Constellation had gained 759 metric tons over its initial estimate, nearly a 13 percent increase. The report attributed part of that growth to underestimating the effect of US Navy technical requirements on a foreign design. Efforts to reduce weight had not prevented the problem from becoming more pronounced as the design matured. Excess weight at entry into service consumes the allowance intended for upgrades across a decades-long career. The result can be reduced combat capability, less room to answer new threats, and a shorter useful service life even before the first ship is complete.

evidence.note: The transcript quotes 759 metric tons of growth, nearly 13 percent, partly caused by underestimated US technical requirements.
The assessment warns that early weight growth can limit later capabilities, adaptation to threats, and planned service life.

segments.title: Requirements control depends on someone empowered to say no
segments.summary: Constellation accumulated well-intentioned improvements without a leader willing to protect the first flight from them.
segments.body: Conspiracy is a less useful explanation than an accumulation of individually sensible improvements proposed by competent people. Without a decision-maker empowered to refuse them, small survivability, system, and capability changes accumulate until the result is a different ship. The deliberately sharp metaphor is the Scrooge in the room, the person who defers a good idea to a later flight because the first ships must enter service. The Arleigh Burke program shows how future configurations can be studied without loading every improvement into the initial design. After cancellation, the same lesson becomes a question of leadership: someone must distinguish a destroyer requirement from a frigate requirement and accept that the appropriate standards may differ. Program discipline controls when each innovation enters the fleet.

evidence.note: The transcript attributes the failure to well-intentioned changes without an effective veto and argues for deferring improvements to later flights.
The closing leadership critique says the responsible authority needed to reject destroyer specifications and reconsider which survivability standards belonged on a frigate.

segments.title: Cancellation follows unsettled design and slow progress
segments.summary: Yard constraints contributed to delay, but continuing design revisions and minimal construction progress provide the deeper explanation for cancellation.
segments.body: Shipyard backlogs and skilled-worker shortages were real constraints, but the Navy knew about them when it placed the order. Work on Constellation began in April 2024, yet the lead ship was reported only 12 percent complete by November 2025. The second ship, Congress, had not been laid down, while revisions left the final appearance and arrangement of both hulls uncertain. The unsettled design appears more decisive than the yard's condition alone. Cancellation became the point at which the Navy had to stop adding time and money to a program whose basic configuration still had not stabilized.

evidence.note: The transcript weighs known yard backlogs and worker shortages against the lead ship's reported 12 percent completion.
Congress had not been laid down, revisions continued, and the conclusion attributes cancellation to the absence of an agreed design.

segments.title: A flotilla frigate only works if the Navy buys it in numbers
segments.summary: The Legend-derived successor is a group operator whose value depends on rapid, sustained production rather than occasional single-ship orders.
segments.body: The replacement effort should learn from Constellation, though its path toward production already shows warning signs. The proposed ship is fundamentally a flotilla vessel that contributes as part of a group rather than acting as a solitary high-end combatant. That role requires enough hulls to be present wherever the fleet needs them. Ordering one ship in scattered years would repeat the procurement instability that weakened FFG-62's economics and industrial base. A basic frigate becomes strategically useful through reliable mass rather than a small number of individually impressive ships.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the successor a flotilla or group-operating vessel and argues that it must be produced quickly and in large numbers rather than in dribs and drabs.

segments.title: Could the US Navy preserve real parent-design commonality?
segments.summary: Any foreign parent design would struggle to remain substantially unchanged under US Navy systems, standards, and institutional habits.
segments.question: Could the US Navy have selected a parent design for Constellation and honestly retained something close to 85 percent commonality with FREMM?
segments.answerShort: Probably not at 85 percent; about 60 percent might have been possible with disciplined changes, but a clean-sheet Perry-style frigate may have fit the Navy better.
segments.body: FREMM itself was not the problem. Roughly 60 percent commonality might have been realistic if American systems were introduced selectively and the Navy adapted its standards to the frigate. Even that outcome is doubtful because the US Navy is institutionally organized to design ships around its own needs and has often done that well. A more honest route may have been to authorize a new American frigate from the outset while treating the Oliver Hazard Perry concept as the governing model. A program should commit either to genuine parent-design restraint or to a clean-sheet design; Constellation paid for the first approach while carrying out the second.

evidence.note: The transcript asks whether 85 percent FREMM commonality was ever honest and proposes about 60 percent as a more plausible target with selective American changes.
The answer emphasizes the Navy's own-design culture and proposes a clean-sheet frigate governed by the original Perry concept.
